metric.why: Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing. Fleet utilization is where the money hides in most enterprise estates, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.
metric.definition: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.

reading.body:
Server utilization rate is the share of provisioned compute doing real work over time, and it is the denominator that makes every other efficiency claim about a data center honest.

The definition insists on time rather than peak, and that distinction carries the weight. A fleet sized for its busiest hour looks fully used at that hour and mostly idle the rest of the day. The idle hours are where power, licenses, and depreciation are spent without producing anything. Measuring at peak conceals that. Measuring over time exposes it.

This is a power fact as much as a cost fact. An idle server draws from the same electrical feed as a busy one, so low utilization means the building, the service entrance, and the cooling are all being paid for at a rate the work does not justify. The sibling metrics, stranded power and space per cabinet and floor loading limits, ask the same question from the physical side: how much of what was built can actually be used.

No utilization figure, target, measurement window, or rule for deciding when a server counts as doing real work is given. A reader cannot learn whether any particular fleet is well or badly used, only that the number should be tracked over time and treated as the baseline against which other efficiency claims are judged.
